------------------------------------------------
FLAT DESIGN

INVARIENTS:

A PORT always has a NET (a special net "unconnected_inports" is provided per-design)
A NET always has a source OUTPORT, which has an INSTANCE ("dummy_source")
an INSTANCE always has a CELL

... that is, a PORT always has describeable behavior.


------------------------------------------------
HEIRARCHICAL DESIGN

The hierarchical design is represented in the form of a verilog
gate-level file (xxx.vg), more generally, by a set of verilog
"modules", which are one-to-one with Sue files; each one represents
one level of hierarchy.  Therefore, it has:

	a type-name
	a list of external connection names, designated as inputs,
		outputs, or inouts; 
	a list of internal wire names;
	a list of instance definitions


type-name :: character-string

exconn-name 
wire-name	::	character_string
		||	character_string [ integer ]
		||	character_string [ integer1 : integer2 ]

    ... the first two forms represent single wires;
	the third form represents an ordered sequence of wires running
	from character_string[integer1] through
	character_string[integer2], inclusive... 
	hence (abs(integer2 - integer1) + 1) wires.


instance-definition	::	instance-name	type-name ( connection-list )

	
instance-name	::	character_string
		||	character_string [ number ]
			

connection-list	::	instance-connection
		||	instance-connection , connection-list

instance-connection	::	type-connection


--------------------------------------------------
DOWNSTREAM TIMING

For static timing purposes, instances are seen as a collection of timing
arcs.  

INPUT-TO-OUTPUT ARC

An edge (rising or falling) arrives at an inport with a given slope
(strictly, transistion time) and delay from T-zero, and propagates
across the arc to emerge on the outport.  The outport is characterized
by its total capacitive load.  Given input slope and output load, the
arc calculates output slope and gate delay.  Gate delay added to input
delay gives ouput delay.

	This model assumes that other inputs are stationary, which 
	is optimistic.

	See below for net delay.

INPUT-TO-CLOCK ARC

As a matter of convenience, flipflop setup time is treated as an
additional stage of delay (can be thought of as path delay internal to
the flipflop). In this case the input slope and the clock slope
determine setup delay that must be added to the path delay in order to
determine whether correct phasing to the clock is being maintained.


GLOBAL TIMING

The DESIGN::global_timing() algorithm seeks to find the long path
through the design.  Each outport is tagged with the worst-case 
delay to that point ... that is, the maximum of 
	(delay at inport + gate delay over an arc)
over all arcs terminating at that outport.

A separate number is calculated for rising edge and falling edge.

The algorithm propagates the worst-case delay from timing sources
(which have delay given) towards destinations.  


TIMING SOURCES:
	the clock inputs to flipflops, which are assumed to have zero
	delay and slope according to the variable "clock_slope" (by
	default tied to "nominal_slope")

	external inputs, which have a delay and slope assigned by the
	"constraints" file. Default is delay = 0 and 
	slope = "nominal_slope". 

		* external slope is fixed, which means that load has
		no effect, which is very optimistic.  Should add an
		external stage with selectable drive strength.

TIMING DESTINATIONS
	non-clock inputs to flipflops

	external outputs, which have a load assigned by the "constraints"
	file.

		* should also be able to define an external delay,
		modeled as a setup time on the external output.


-------------------------------------

DOWNSTREAM

The DOWNSTREAM class reprents an ordered list of instances which are
"downstream" (in the signal propagation direction) from a set of root
instances. For global_timing, the root set is all timing sources.
For computeing timing slack, the root set may be an individual
instance or the instance set of a clone.

The list is constructed by doing a depth-first tree traversal from
source (inports) to destination (outports).  When a leaf node 
(timing destination instance) is encountered or when an intermediate
node (instance) is completed, it is pushed onto the list.

A flag is kept in each instance to show whether the instance has
already been pushed onto the list. If the traversal enters a node
where the flag is set, it returns immediately without pushing the
instance a second time. 

We have to watch out for circular dependencies.  So when the algorithm
first enters an instance, it sets the flag to a value indicating
IN_PROGRESS, and then descends into downstream nodes.  If the
algorithm enters an instance where the flag is set to IN_PROGRESS,
then there is a circular path. The algorithm does what it can, which 
is to provide a warning message and return immediately, without
getting caught in a loop.

Thus, in the resulting ordered list, each instance will come after
all its timing dependencies, and before all its timing dependents.


    clear all flags
    for each instance in root_instances,
      instance->find_downstream_instances;
    done
  
  INSTANCE::find_downstream_instances:
    if flag equals DONE
      return

    if flag equals IN_PROGRESS
      message "circular path detected"
      return

    if this is timing destination,
      set flag to DONE
      push this onto list
      return
  
    else
      set flag to IN_PROGRESS
      for each outport in outportlist,
        net = outport->net;
        for each inport in net->inportlist,
          next_instance = inport->instance;
          next_instance->find_downstream_instances;
      push this onto list
      set flag to DONE
      return  


GLOBAL TIMING

Having constructed a global_downstream instance, the global timing
algorithm can evaluate each instance in the list order.  The timing
delay at the timing sources is known as initial conditions; as each
instance is encountered, the worst-case delay to each of its inputs is
known.  The timing model for the instance is used to construt a set of
timing delays along all the arcs; for each outport, the worst timing
delay is saved as the worst-case delay at that point.  That delay is
propagated along the connected net (adding a value for net delay if
desired) to the inputs of the directly-downstream instances.

  for each instance in global_downstream instancelist sequentially,
    for each outport in instance->outportlist,
      set worst-case_delay = 0
      for each timing arcs ending at this outport
        compute gate_delay from timing arc
        compute total_delay = gate_delay + related_inport->total_delay 
        if total_delay > worst-case_delay,
          worst-case_delay = total_delay
  set design_long_path_delay = 0
  for each instance in timing_destinations,
    if timing_destination->worst-case_delay > design_long_path_delay,
      set design_long_path_delay = timing_destination->worst_case_delay
      set design_long_path_destination = timing_destination
  done


COMPUTING TIMING SLACK

For a given instance, define the timing slack as the maximum delay
that can be added to all paths through the instance without impacting
the design long path.  

Begin by performing a global_timing, so that the design long path and
the worst-case delays to all inports are known. Then for the given
instance, find the downstream instances (construct a DOWNSTREAM) as
above, and do the timing algorithm described above... in this case it
is a partial timing, since only instances downstream of the given
instance are evaluated. (*Note, these values are stored in a way that
doesn't damage the stored global timing values.)  Not every timing
destinations in the design will be encountered, so keep track of which
timing destination encountered has the largest delay.  At the end,
that delay is the delay of the longest path that goes through the
given instance; that value subtracted from the design long path delay
gives the desired timing slack.


USING THE TIMING SLACK TO DOWNSIZE AN INSTANCES

(Assuming a smaller cell is available,) compute the timing slack 
as above. If the timing slack is not greater than the
minimum_desireable_slack, return.

Duplicate a three-gate path through the instance; time it.  Replace
the instance with the smaller instance; time the path again.  The
difference is a first guess at how much slack the downsize will
consume; if the timing_slack minus that value is not greater than 
the minimum_desireable_slack, return.

Replace the instance in the design structure with the smaller size and
recalculate the timing slack. Again if the minimum_desireable_slack
will not be maintained, return.

We are now OK with keeping this change, but the global_timing
worst-case delays may not be too small for the downstream instances. 
So we have to walk over this instances downstreams recalculating
the global delay.


DOWNSIZEING CLONES

Most similar to above; the downstream root-instance list is set to 
the clone's instance list.  The three-gate path is constructed for a
random instance, and if that looks good, the entire clone is replaced,
the downstream timing recalculated, &c..


THE HIGH-LEVEL ALGORITHMS

User-level commands are availabe to downsize by instances, by clones,
or a named instance.

Experience shows that the most efficient thing to do is to downsize
the largest instances first, so the algorithm actually makes several
passes over the design instancelist, first trying to downsize all the
E-sizes, then D-sizes and so on.
